1290.bp: Recommender systems make suggestions to billions of people every day, but they often misunderstand *why* someone clicks or buys. Sometimes you genuinely want something; other times you click because your friends did, or because it seemed socially expected. If a system can't tell these two reasons apart, it will either push too hard on social trends or miss what you actually care about.
1290.wh: When you feed raw text to a language model (LLM) about products, it learns to predict clicks accurately, but accuracy masks a deeper problem: the model fuses together these different reasons into one black box. If you later ask the system to explain why it recommended something, the explanation points to attention weights—how much the model focused on each word—but those weights don't actually tell you which reason (genuine interest or social pressure) drove the decision. Fixing the fusion doesn't help if your explanation mechanism is fundamentally unreliable.
1290.ap: DisCoRec splits the recommendation task into separate branches, each handling a different reason for clicks (genuine intent, social conformity, and others). Each branch gets its own semantic understanding of products via an LLM, then a gating mechanism—controlled by the LLM as well—decides how much to trust each branch's signal when making the final prediction. The system learns which branch matters most for each user.
1290.ww: By training the branches independently but letting them compare their opinions through the gate, the model can learn that some users are swayed by trends while others ignore them entirely. The LLM provides semantic grounding (understanding what a product actually *is*) to each branch, and the gate learns to weight them honestly rather than hiding the decision in opaque attention patterns.
1290.po: On real data from Amazon, DisCoRec improved prediction accuracy by about 5% over existing methods, and crucially, the explanations now reliably show which factor—genuine intent or social pressure—drove each recommendation. This matters for transparency and for tuning systems to respect different user values.

1291.bp: Software engineers spend enormous amounts of time searching through code repositories to understand what a fix should do. A system that can automatically suggest patches to fix bugs should ideally be smart about what it looks up, but today's best systems waste massive effort retrieving and re-reading code that won't help the fix.
1291.wh: When a code agent tries to patch a bug, it has two jobs: finding the relevant code (exploration) and writing the fix (patching). Current systems bundle these together, so when the agent misunderstands what to look for, it wastes tokens—the billable unit of computation—fetching irrelevant files. Experiments show that exploration alone consumes up to 56% of all computational tokens, yet this part barely improves with bigger, more expensive models.
1291.ap: SAGE uses a small, fast model trained specifically for code search, working as a tool for a separate, frozen large model that handles patching. The search model is first trained by watching a strong agent explore repositories, learning which files typically matter. Then reinforcement learning refines it further by asking: does the code you found actually help with patching? The search model gets rewarded only for retrieving context the patcher can use.
1291.ww: By splitting the tasks, you can make the search model small and fast without sacrificing quality. It learns not just which files are similar to the query, but which files contain the *actionable information* a patcher needs—a much tighter target than generic retrieval quality. This is learned through direct feedback on whether the retrieved context led to a successful patch.
1291.po: On a challenging benchmark (SWE-bench Verified), SAGE reduced the computational cost of exploration by 67% while actually improving the rate at which it found valid patches. Overall inference cost dropped 21%, making automated code patching far more practical for real deployment.

1292.bp: Advertisers and recommenders need to predict whether users will click on ads in real time. The problem: those predictions require user data so sensitive (age, location, search history) that companies can't safely send it to cloud servers. One solution is cryptography—encrypt the data so tightly that the server can't read it, yet can still do the math to generate a prediction.
1292.wh: Homomorphic encryption lets you compute on encrypted data without ever decrypting it, but the math is ferociously expensive. Especially for recommendation models, you often need to compute second-order interactions between features—essentially, does age combined with location create a signal? Naively doing this through homomorphic encryption requires computing every pair of features, a cost that balloons quadratically with the number of features.
1292.ap: HE-DeepFM redesigns the Factorization Machine (a standard recommendation component) to work efficiently inside encrypted math. Instead of computing all pairs explicitly, it exploits a packing trick in the encryption scheme (CKKS SIMD) to compute multiple interactions at once, bundling related feature pairs into single encrypted operations. The system then prunes less critical bootstrapping steps—expensive re-encryption operations—that normally dominate computation time.
1292.ww: By understanding how the encryption scheme's parallelism works, the team aligned the model's structure to that parallelism. The Factorization Machine's internal math maps naturally to batched encrypted operations, and you can skip some intermediate encryption steps if the model is small enough. This is a first-principles redesign, not just a generic speed hack.
1292.po: On real ad-click data (Criteo), HE-DeepFM ran 2.85 times faster than the naive encrypted approach, and for small models, eliminated expensive re-encryption entirely. Prediction accuracy stayed the same, so companies can now offer encrypted inference without sacrificing either safety or speed.

1293.bp: Imagine analyzing a text conversation where someone is upset. To truly help them, a system needs to recognize the emotion (are they sad or angry?), trace why they feel that way (did someone's comment trigger it?), and then respond with genuine support rather than canned advice. Current systems handle each of these as separate boxes, losing the bigger picture.
1293.wh: Conversational emotion understanding involves three linked steps: sensing emotions from tone and word choice, finding which prior comments caused them, and generating supportive responses. Existing methods treat these independently, so the emotion detector can't pass its confidence down to the cause finder, and the responder doesn't know how certain the causes were. Additionally, real conversations mix text, voice tone, and facial expressions—but most systems just concatenate these three modalities crudely rather than capturing how they interact.
1293.ap: GraphEMO models the three steps as a chain where each builds on the previous one. Emotion perception feeds into cause extraction (which can only find causes for emotions it recognized), which feeds into response generation. To handle multimodal information richly, it builds graphs representing relationships between speakers and modalities—which speakers are talking to whom, which parts of text align with which voice tones or facial expressions—and uses graph attention to reason across these relationships.
1293.ww: By chaining the tasks and sharing learned representations, each step can specialize: the first stage is alert to any hint of emotion, the second refines by looking only at detected emotions, and the third grounds its response in causes the prior stages validated. The graph capture genuine structural relationships—speaker A directed their comment at speaker B, not C—making the multimodal fusion structured rather than a naive concatenation.
1293.po: GraphEMO achieved the best results on multiple emotion benchmarks, consistently improving over prior methods across different underlying language models (Qwen and LLaMA). Real tests showed it accurately traces causes and generates contextually appropriate emotional support.

1294.bp: Search is evolving from single keywords ('paris hotels') to longer, conversational questions ('I'm looking for a pet-friendly hotel in Paris near the Eiffel Tower within walking distance'). These complex queries are harder to generate automatically, but creating good examples is costly—you need humans to write them.
1294.wh: Traditional datasets assume users type single short queries, but real people with voice assistants or conversational search ask full narratives. Humans can naturally piece together a complex need across multiple related searches ('where's a good vegan restaurant in Paris, also what's nearby?'), but an automatic system can't just generate random long text—it must build narratives that reflect how actual people search.
1294.ap: The method takes raw short queries from search logs and clusters similar ones together to form synthetic search sessions (a sequence of related queries). It then takes these sessions and generates a single long narrative that stitches them together into a coherent story of what the user was looking for. The process learned from patterns in real user behavior.
1294.ww: Real search behavior is inherently structured: people don't query random topics; they follow threads (restaurant search leads to questions about neighborhoods, which leads to transit questions). By clustering related short queries into sessions first, the system captures this natural structure before generating the narrative, avoiding nonsensical long queries.
1294.po: Human raters tested the result: 44% of automatically generated narratives were indistinguishable from human-written ones, suggesting the system learned to mimic genuine search behavior convincingly. These narratives were used in an official competition (TREC 2025) to benchmark how well large language models handle complex, long-form question answering.

1295.bp: When you search in one language but want results in another (searching in English for Spanish documents), or when you need answers across multiple languages simultaneously, the system must find the right documents even though the query and results may use completely different words for the same concept.
1295.wh: Traditional dense retrieval in English uses fine-grained statistics about which individual words (or sub-word tokens) in the results are most relevant. But modern systems have traded away this token-level detail to improve speed and reduce memory. Without it, you can't use the old method—picking specific expansion terms—when crossing language boundaries, where a direct word match is unlikely anyway.
1295.ap: The method clusters retrieved documents to identify groups of similar content, then uses the cluster centers as pseudo-terms to expand the query, even when you can't see which individual words matter. It compares different clustering techniques (standard clustering versus HDBScan, which is better at finding weird-shaped groups) and tests how well the resulting expansion works for retrieval across languages or languages.
1295.ww: Cluster centers capture semantic meaning (a point representing 'restaurant in Paris') without requiring individual word statistics. As long as the clusters themselves are good, the system can decide which clusters are worth including in the expansion, and this decision still helps retrieval even when query and results use different languages.
1295.po: On multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval benchmarks (including TREC 2024 NeuCLIR tasks), the clustering-based expansion improved retrieval quality compared to baselines. The flexibility to use different clustering methods also opens paths to optimization for specific language pairs or search settings.

1296.bp: When a system generates a caption for an image ('a dog jumping over a fence'), it grounds the caption in external examples—finding similar images and borrowing descriptions from them. But this only works well if the system looks at the same level of detail as the caption needs. If the caption needs to mention a small bird in the background, but the system only compares whole-image similarity, it might miss that detail entirely.
1296.wh: Whole-image retrieval is fast and simple but sees images at only one scale. A cluttered scene with multiple objects gets reduced to a single similarity score, so rare or small objects disappear. Patch-level (region-level) retrieval would be better, but it's expensive: breaking the image into patches and retrieving separately for each one balloons the computational cost.
1296.ap: PeaCap divides the query image into patches (rectangular sections), retrieves similar patches independently to find objects, collects object tags from the retrieved results, and then fuses these tags with the whole-image understanding through a lightweight module trained alongside a frozen large language model. The fusion learns to weight the patch-level and whole-image signals appropriately.
1296.ww: Patch retrieval is more likely to surface small or rare objects because it looks at localized context. But you don't need to retrieval independently for every patch—you can do it just often enough to cover the scene. The lightweight fusion module learns to blend patch insights (detailed object coverage) with whole-image context (overall scene structure), getting the best of both without the full computational cost.
1296.po: On standard caption benchmarks (COCO) and out-of-domain images, PeaCap generated captions with competitive quality, capturing more objects and details than whole-image-only retrieval, all while using only lightweight training (freezing the base language model).

1297.bp: Small language models deployed to low-resource languages (Thai, Vietnamese) need to decide when to call a tool—like a calculator or web search—to help answer a question. But they often call tools when they shouldn't (for questions no tool can solve), leading to hallucinated answers. Teaching them to refuse correctly is critical but underexplored in multilingual settings.
1297.wh: Naively adding more refusal examples to training paradoxically hurts: the model learns to say 'no' more often, but then also stops calling tools correctly. Language models in low-resource languages have weaker understanding of what tools exist and when they apply. Additionally, standard evaluation misleads you—it counts badly formatted tool calls as refusals, inflating success scores by 30 percentage points when the model actually tried to call a tool.
1297.ap: The method teaches the model to generate structured reasoning about whether to call each tool. Rather than just learning to say yes or no, the model learns to work through stages: first, understand what the user is actually asking; second, assess whether any available tool could help; third, evaluate the risk of hallucination if no tool helps. This reasoning is done through lightweight schemas (templates) that don't add much computation.
1297.ww: By making reasoning explicit, the model internalizes the decision process. It's harder to shortcut (just say no) when you're forced to explain why each tool won't help. The structured templates also keep the reasoning interpretable and steerable—you can see where the model went wrong.
1297.po: On new benchmarks for Vietnamese and Thai (1-billion-parameter models), structured reasoning training improved refusal accuracy significantly. The paper also exposed the evaluation flaw, showing that previous systems scored much higher than they should have, which refocuses the field on the real problem.

1298.bp: Named entity recognition (NER) systems learn to label words in text—marking 'Paris' as a location or 'Apple' as a company. In real deployment, new entity types appear over time (a startup's name is never in the old training data). The system must learn to recognize new types without forgetting old ones, a classic dilemma: learn too hard on new data and you erase old knowledge; hold on too tight to old knowledge and you miss new entities.
1298.wh: When you learn new entity types, the model's internal weights shift, degrading performance on old types—a problem called forgetting. One defense is memory replay: keep some old examples and interleave them during training. But if new entity types are rare in the old examples, the model won't learn to handle them well. Another defense is knowledge distillation: force the new model to match the old model's outputs. But which parts of the old model are critical? Using all of them wastes capacity on outdated knowledge.
1298.ap: The method identifies which neurons (internal decision units) in the model are critical for old tasks using gradient-based importance scores, then constrains those neurons to stay close to their old values when learning new tasks via a distillation loss. In parallel, it maintains a memory buffer with examples of all entity types seen so far, including their learned features, and uses a hybrid loss that balances learning new types while respecting the buffer's old knowledge.
1298.ww: By computing importance per neuron, you preserve what actually matters for old tasks without locking down irrelevant parts of the model. Neurons critical for location recognition aren't the same as those for person names, so you can let person-name neurons adapt freely while protecting location neurons. The memory buffer with learned features (not just raw text) captures the gist of what the model learned about each entity type.
1298.po: On standard continual NER benchmarks, the method outperformed existing continual learning baselines, especially on macro-F1 scores (which emphasize rare entity types). The system successfully learned new entity types while holding old knowledge stable.

1299.bp: Knowledge graphs are databases of facts (Paris is a city, it's in France, it has the Eiffel Tower). Entities in different knowledge graphs can represent the same thing (Paris in one graph, 'París' in another) but use different names and languages. Multi-modal entity alignment finds these equivalences by mixing information from structure (which facts connect them), attributes (what properties they have), and images (what they look like). The catch: real-world graphs have missing pieces—some entities have no image, or incomplete attribute data—forcing the system to guess.
1299.wh: When you impute missing data (guess what's missing), those guesses can be noisy or outright wrong. A system that blindly trusts all imputed data propagates that noise through the fusion step, corrupting the entire alignment. The intuition seems right—when uncertain about an imputed value, should you just not trust it?—but quantifying that uncertainty is hard, and using it to discount noise is even harder.
1299.ap: SURE imputes missing features using a probabilistic model that explicitly tracks uncertainty—how confident is this guess? Then, instead of treating all imputed features the same, it uses a gating mechanism (a learned filter) controlled by the uncertainty estimates to suppress features that are likely wrong. It also modifies the learning objective to be uncertainty-aware, so the model doesn't waste effort fitting to unreliable imputed values.
1299.ww: Uncertainty quantification turns a binary (imputed yes/no) into a continuous signal (how trustworthy is this imputation?). By gating the fusion, you let the model learn when to ignore uncertain features. The learning objective modification prevents the model from over-fitting to noise, which is especially important in highly uncertain scenarios.
1299.po: On multi-modal entity alignment benchmarks (DBP15K), SURE significantly outperformed existing methods, and crucially, it maintained strong performance even when 50%+ of modalities were missing—a scenario where baselines collapsed. The method showed the practical importance of tracking imputation uncertainty.

1300.bp: Multi-agent social simulations use multiple large language models, each playing a different character, to simulate how societies respond to policies or crises. These simulations capture emergent behavior (characters learn from each other, conflicts arise naturally), but running them is expensive—each character's reasoning consumes tokens like a user typing in ChatGPT.
1300.wh: The cost grows with the number of agents: more characters means more conversations, more reasoning, and higher token bills. But not every agent contributes equally—some might repeat the same stance, others might not affect the outcome. Naively removing agents breaks the simulation's realism. The challenge is to find the minimum set of agents you need while keeping the simulation's social dynamics intact.
1300.ap: SocialDropout assigns an importance weight to each agent, learned via reinforcement learning. The learning objective minimizes two things: the computational cost (token count, execution time) and the number of agents, while ensuring the simulation remains realistic. Each round of the simulation, the most important agents are selected for reasoning, while less critical ones are skipped or contribute passively.
1300.ww: By training a reward function that directly penalizes cost and sparsity but rewards realism, the system learns which agents drive meaningful interactions. A character who repeats others or occupies a minor role gets lower importance, while pivotal characters get higher weights. The key insight is that social dynamics are often driven by a small core of agents, not everyone.
1300.po: Experiments showed that SocialDropout reduced agent participation substantially while maintaining behavioral realism and outcome consistency. The simulation stayed believable despite cutting many agents, demonstrating that most of a simulation's value comes from a targeted subset of well-chosen characters.

1301.bp: Music theory questions often require multiple steps: 'What key is this piece in, and how many modulations occur?' requires scanning a score, identifying the key signature, tracking when it changes, and then reasoning about why the composer chose those changes. Existing systems treat music retrieval as a lookup problem, but these compositional questions need chaining multiple analyses.
1301.wh: Large language models were trained on text, not sheet music notation. A score—with its staves, clefs, time signatures, and note sequences—encodes information very differently than English text. LLMs struggle to parse long structured documents and reliably chain multiple reasoning steps over them without hallucinating facts about music they don't understand.
1301.ap: CSyMR-Agent combines an LLM with deterministic tools built from music21 (a symbolic music library). The tools can extract facts reliably: 'list all key changes in this score', 'count how many measures have polyphony', 'find all instances of this melodic motif'. The agent uses a ReAct framework—reasoning aloud, then calling tools, then using results to refine reasoning—to answer complex questions by chaining tool calls.
1301.ww: By delegating to deterministic, trustworthy tools for music analysis, the system avoids hallucinations. The LLM's role becomes reasoning about music concepts and planning which tools to call, not inventing facts. The ReAct structure (reason-execute-act-think) lets the system backtrack if a tool result contradicts earlier reasoning.
1301.po: The benchmark CSyMR-Bench includes 126 questions from real user discussions and professional exams, where answers require chaining multiple analytical steps. Agent-based systems outperformed pure prompting baselines, especially when given access to well-designed symbolic analysis tools. This opens new ground for LLM-based music education and analysis.

1302.bp: Internet memes—images with text and references—communicate through layers of implied meaning. A meme about a movie character might reference the plot, the actor's real life, a prior meme, and current events all at once. Understanding it requires not just seeing the image, but grasping ambiguous visual metaphors and weaving in broader social context.
1302.wh: Current approaches treat understanding as a deterministic process: look at the image, decode the meaning. But memes are inherently ambiguous—different viewers might interpret them differently, and the interpretation depends on what you know about current events, internet culture, and the original reference. If the system makes a wrong initial guess (misidentifying which reference the meme is using), that error cascades: all downstream reasoning builds on the wrong foundation.
1302.ap: SEED reformulates meme understanding as an energy minimization problem in a semantic space. It builds a tree of possible interpretations, then iteratively refines them. An Evaluator Agent quantifies how self-consistent each interpretation is using an energy function (high energy = contradictory, low energy = coherent). A Supplier Agent retrieves external context and prior memes. A Reasoner Agent refines explanations. The system repeatedly moves toward lower-energy (more consistent) interpretations, like a ball rolling down a hill.
1302.ww: Energy minimization captures the intuition that good interpretations should be internally consistent and grounded in evidence. By explicitly measuring inconsistency (energy) and providing structured feedback (gradient), the system can correct early mistakes. An interpretation that seemed plausible initially might reveal contradictions as the system digs deeper.
1302.po: SEED outperformed baselines on multiple meme understanding tasks, especially benefiting from the iterative refinement. By treating understanding as a search for internally consistent explanations rather than one-shot decoding, the system reduced hallucinations and improved alignment with human interpretations.

1303.bp: Multi-agent systems maintain shared memory: as agents discuss a problem over hours or days, they record decisions, discoveries, and agreements. But as the problem evolves, earlier decisions get revised, retracted, or contradicted. When a new agent joins or the system needs to summarize, it must decide: which claims are still valid? Has that decision been superseded?
1303.wh: Most summarization treats memory as a simple pool of facts to aggregate. But in multi-agent systems, memory is non-monotonic—facts can change truth value over time. An agent might claim 'we should use Strategy A' (true at 2 PM), then later say 'actually Strategy B is better' (false by 3 PM, true by 4 PM). Simple summarization conflates these, producing summaries that mix valid and outdated claims into nonsense.
1303.ap: EvoMem reconstructs the timeline of how memory evolved. It retrieves all past claims and decisions, identifies key timepoints where something changed, and summarizes what was believed at each point. Crucially, it orders timepoints by causality and decides which changes supersede prior claims. The output is an evolutionary timeline showing not just 'what we know now' but 'how our understanding changed'.
1303.ww: By explicitly modeling time and causality, the system can distinguish between 'this claim was true, then retracted' and 'this claim is simply outdated noise'. Agents can use the timeline to understand the reasoning behind current positions—why did we move from Strategy A to B?—rather than just getting a snapshot of the present.
1303.po: On a new benchmark with controlled revisions and retractions, EvoMem consistently improved accuracy and suppressed outdated errors compared to baselines using long-context retrieval or standard summarization. The approach is practical, adding minimal overhead while significantly clarifying agent memory.

1304.bp: Recommender systems can be built by training a model to predict the next item a user will engage with, just like language models predict the next word. The system generates a sequence of recommended item identifiers (like a 'product code'), and the user sees them as suggestions. The catch: with millions of items, naively predicting each one sequentially is slow, requiring many forward passes.
1304.wh: Existing systems use a trie—a tree of valid item sequences—and generate identifiers one-at-a-time with hard constraints forcing the output to stay on valid paths. This is locally greedy: if the first identifier predicted is sub-optimal, all subsequent predictions are locked into sub-optimal branches. By the time the model realizes a mistake, it's too late to backtrack.
1304.ap: OneGR computes all positions' predictions in a single forward pass (no iteration), producing scores for every possible item at every position simultaneously. It then encodes the space of valid item sequences as a weighted graph (transducer) and uses A* search to find the globally best sequence, using the one-pass scores as guidance. The search explores only reachable valid sequences, avoiding impossible ones.
1304.ww: Computing everything at once lets the model consider global trade-offs: maybe position-1 should sacrifice a bit of score to open better options for positions 2 and 3. A* search finds the globally optimal sequence under the one-pass scores, sidestepping the local-greedy trap. The transducer ensures only valid sequences are considered, keeping the search tractable.
1304.po: OneGR outperformed baseline generative recommendation systems on multiple benchmarks. By eliminating iterative decoding and using structured search, it became both faster and more accurate—a rare win-win in machine learning.
